explanation: Modern computer systems employ a memory hierarchy to bridge the speed gap between CPU and main memory.  This hierarchy consists of multiple levels of storage with varying speeds and capacities, ranging from fast, small registers and caches to slower, larger main memory and disk.  Caching strategies aim to exploit locality of reference (temporal and spatial) to keep frequently accessed data closer to the CPU, minimizing memory access latency and improving performance.  Effective use of the memory hierarchy is crucial for optimizing application speed.
syntax: Cache organization typically involves set-associative mapping with LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement policy.  Specific details vary by architecture (e.g., cache size, associativity, line size).  Compiler optimizations and memory allocation strategies can significantly impact cache utilization.

; If array elements are close in memory, multiple elements may reside in the same cache line, reducing cache misses.
example_explanation: This example demonstrates spatial locality.  Accessing array elements sequentially leads to a higher probability that consecutive elements are already in the cache (or brought into the cache together). This avoids multiple memory accesses, considerably speeding up execution compared to accessing array elements randomly.  The efficiency directly depends on the cache line size, which determines how many consecutive bytes are brought into the cache together.  Poor memory access patterns (e.g., accessing elements far apart) can lead to a high number of cache misses, degrading performance significantly.
